title: The Portrait of Saint Alder's Again
premise: Oscar Dravenmoor, an insurance investigator whose photographic memory has kept her professionally untouchable and personally invisible, is called to Saint Alder's estate when a stranger is found dead wearing clothes lifted from her own closet. The murder is a message: someone from the Alder circle she investigated thirty years ago—a case she closed by burying what she remembered—wants her to become the story instead of its silent witness. As the anniversary dinner of the old scandal approaches, Oscar's flawless recall becomes both weapon and liability, forcing her to reconstruct the alibis she once accepted too easily. In the end, she exposes the killer as the one person whose memory she trusted over her own—her former mentor—and chooses, for the first time, to be seen.
about_author: Casper Sterling is the pen name of a former claims adjuster who spent eleven years reading other people's disasters before writing them. They live in a coastal town much like Saint Alder's, where they keep meticulous notes on everyone they meet.

chapters.title: The Man in My Coat
chapters.summary: Oscar Dravenmoor arrives at the Alder estate to assess a routine claim and finds a dead man dressed in clothes stolen from her own apartment closet. Told in her precise, cataloguing POV, the chapter establishes her photographic memory as armor. Emotional beat: cold professionalism cracking into genuine fear—the first time in thirty years she has been seen.

chapters.title: Thirty Years of Perfect Recall
chapters.summary: A flashback-laced chapter in which Oscar reviews her files on the 1995 Alder fire that killed patriarch Edmund Alder, a case she closed after accepting four immaculate alibis. Her mentor, Inspector Vance Corliss, taught her that some memories are better filed than spoken. Emotional beat: unease—she realizes she never questioned why he wanted it closed.

chapters.title: The Widow Who Remembers Nothing
chapters.summary: Oscar interviews Vivienne Alder, now eighty and sharp-eyed despite claiming senility, who recognizes Oscar instantly and says, 'You were the girl in the doorway.' POV alternates between Oscar's interview notes and her intrusive memories. Emotional beat: dread—Vivienne knows something about the night of the fire that Oscar herself has never said aloud.

chapters.title: Alibi Number One: The Gardener
chapters.summary: Oscar tracks down Tomas Reyes, the estate gardener whose alibi placed him at the train station the night of the fire; his ticket stub was the anchor of the whole case. Now dying of emphysema, he confesses the stub wasn't his—it was given to him. Emotional beat: vertigo, as the foundation of Oscar's proudest closure begins to crumble.

chapters.title: A Photograph That Shouldn't Exist
chapters.summary: Searching the dead man's effects, Oscar finds a photograph of herself at twenty-two, standing outside the Alder boathouse—an image that exists nowhere in her own perfect memory. Whose POV: Oscar, increasingly doubting the infallibility that defines her. Emotional beat: identity shaken—if her memory can be edited, who is she?

chapters.title: The Anniversary Dinner Invitation
chapters.summary: An engraved invitation arrives: the Alder family requests Oscar attend the thirtieth-anniversary dinner commemorating Edmund's death. The dead man's fingerprints are on the envelope. Emotional beat: trap snapping shut—refusing means losing access; accepting means walking into a room full of suspects who expect her.

chapters.title: Alibi Number Two: The Heir
chapters.summary: Julian Alder, Edmund's son and now the family's public face, gives Oscar a polished account of the night—but his story contains a detail only someone inside the house could know. Oscar says nothing, filing it away. Emotional beat: predatory calm returning; the investigator in her wakes up hungry.

chapters.title: What the Boathouse Kept
chapters.summary: Oscar breaks into the restored boathouse from the photograph and finds a hidden compartment containing Edmund's real will, which disinherited everyone in favor of an unnamed ward. Emotional beat: revelation and danger—footsteps on the dock force her to flee with the document half-photographed in her mind.

chapters.title: Vance Comes to Town
chapters.summary: Her old mentor appears unannounced, offering help and gently suggesting she drop the case for her own good. His charm hasn't aged, but Oscar notices he still wears the same watch stopped at 11:47—the estimated time of the fire. Emotional beat: poisoned nostalgia; gratitude curdling into suspicion.

chapters.title: Alibi Number Three: The Housekeeper
chapters.summary: Marisol Finch, the housekeeper whose testimony placed all four suspects in separate rooms, is found alive but terrified, packing to leave town. She tells Oscar that Corliss coached every statement. Emotional beat: grief and fury—the case wasn't solved, it was authored.

chapters.title: The Ward
chapters.summary: Digging into adoption records, Oscar discovers Edmund's secret ward was a child orphaned in the same fire's aftermath—a child placed with a foster family in Oscar's own hometown. The chapter ends on the birthdate. Emotional beat: the floor dropping out—Oscar begins to suspect the will names her.

chapters.title: Dinner Rehearsal
chapters.summary: At a tense pre-dinner gathering, Julian announces a new memorial wing funded by 'recovered assets,' and Vivienne publicly asks Oscar to say a few words about the investigation. Someone slips a note into her coat: 'He remembers everything too.' Emotional beat: claustrophobia—every guest is performing, and she can't tell for whom.

chapters.title: Alibi Number Four: The Daughter
chapters.summary: Cordelia Alder, estranged and living abroad, returns early and confronts Oscar privately: she saw Corliss on the grounds the night of the fire and has stayed silent for thirty years out of fear. Emotional beat: alliance forming—two women deciding, finally, to stop being witnesses and become investigators.

chapters.title: The Edited Memory
chapters.summary: Oscar interrogates her own recollection of the night she stood 'in the doorway' at age twenty-two and finds seams—details too neat, gaps too smooth. She realizes Corliss spent months after the fire feeding her a curated version of events, exploiting her trust in her own mind. Emotional beat: horror turned inward; her gift revealed as a wound.

chapters.title: Marisol Doesn't Make the Ferry
chapters.summary: Marisol is found drowned hours before she was set to testify, ruled accidental. The police, led by Corliss's protégé, close the file in a day. Emotional beat: rage and resolve—the killer isn't hiding anymore; the murders are messages aimed squarely at Oscar.

chapters.title: Reconstructing the Fire
chapters.summary: In a tour-de-force sequence, Oscar rebuilds the true timeline of 1995 from fragments: Edmund discovered insurance fraud run by Corliss himself, and died for it; the four alibis were stitched together to protect the investigator, not the family. Emotional beat: cold clarity—the case she closed was the crime.

chapters.title: The Dead Man's Name
chapters.summary: Oscar finally identifies the corpse: a retired archivist Corliss hired decades ago to manage the fraud's paper trail, killed when he tried to blackmail his employer. Among his papers: the original photograph of young Oscar, taken by Corliss the night of the fire. Emotional beat: sickening understanding—she was always part of the cover-up, chosen because of her memory.

chapters.title: The Night Before the Anniversary
chapters.summary: Corliss visits Oscar's room, all warmth and menace, admitting obliquely that he made her career and can unmake her: 'You remember everything, Oscar. Imagine what people would believe you remembered.' Emotional beat: terror at her greatest strength weaponized against her—her testimony is worthless because her mind is known to be compromised.

chapters.title: The Anniversary Dinner
chapters.summary: The climax: at the dinner, Oscar rises to speak and instead lays out the reconstructed crime before forty guests, using the hall itself—each alibi assigned to the room where it was fabricated. Corliss, cornered, moves to silence her physically; Cordelia and Julian intervene as the truth detonates the family's mythology. Emotional beat: triumphant exposure—visibility as victory.

chapters.title: Confession at 11:47
chapters.summary: In custody, Corliss tries his final gambit: convincing Oscar the boathouse will and the ward records are fabrications she invented. But she produces the one thing he couldn't edit—her contemporaneous childhood diary, matching the will's details. Emotional beat: quiet devastation; the mentor's fall witnessed without mercy or gloating.

chapters.title: The Ward Is Named
chapters.summary: The will is validated: Edmund left his estate to the orphaned child—Oscar herself, placed nearby deliberately so someone might one day look again at the case. She must decide whether to claim a name and inheritance built on tragedy. Emotional beat: bittersweet reckoning with identity—she was never invisible, only unread.

chapters.title: Portrait of a Witness
chapters.summary: Weeks later, Oscar hangs a commissioned portrait of Edmund in the restored boathouse and donates most of the inheritance to Marisol's family and the archive Corliss burned. She takes a new case—not as the invisible investigator, but under her own name. Emotional beat: resolution and rebirth; memory reclaimed not as armor, but as authorship.
